stops.name: Medina, at the Prophet's tomb
stops.campa: From Mecca, Attar rides north to Medina, to the mosque and the green dome that shelter the grave of the Prophet Muhammad, and prays there as every pilgrim on this road has prayed since the first century of the faith. Every book he will write in old age opens, in the manner of his time, with praise of this same Prophet before a word of Sufi doctrine is set down; the visit fixes, in a man already deep in his thirties, the frame within which the whole of his later mysticism will be argued: never outside the faith, always toward its innermost room.

stops.name: Baghdad, the execution ground of Hallaj
stops.campa: In Baghdad, Attar seeks out the ground where, two hundred and fifty years before, Mansur al-Hallaj was flogged, mutilated, crucified and burned for crying in the streets ana'l-Haqq, I am the Truth, a claim that scandalized the jurists as blasphemy and that the Sufis after him have never stopped turning over as the boldest utterance of a soul drowned in God. Attar gathers here every surviving word of the affair, and will give Hallaj the longest single life in his book of the saints, closing the whole memorial with him, martyr and touchstone, as if no one after him could be added to the list.

stops.name: Basra, the grave of Rabia
stops.campa: South to Basra, river-city of dates and grammarians, Attar visits the grave of Rabia al-Adawiyya, the freed slave-woman four centuries dead whose love of God, she always said, asked nothing of Paradise and feared nothing of Hell, and wanted only Him. Of all the saints he will gather into his book, hers is the one woman's life set beside the men's without apology or qualification, her sayings on love without transaction copied down here as carefully as any shaykh's. He leaves Basra carrying, without yet knowing what shape it will take, the seed of a doctrine of love that will carry thirty birds across seven valleys to their king.

stops.name: Gorganj, the circle of Majd al-Din Baghdadi
stops.campa: The road turns north and east, into Khwarizm, to Gorganj, capital of a Sultan who does not yet know he will one day provoke the ruin of the whole eastern world. Here, by his own later word, the only teacher-claim of Attar's life scholars will accept as more than legend, he meets Majd al-Din Baghdadi, a master of the young Kubrawi order founded by Najm al-Din Kubra. The meeting is brief, a single encounter Attar himself confirms rather than a discipleship he claims, but it is enough: he returns toward Khorasan carrying the imprint of a living order, not only the dead saints' sayings, on his mystical formation.

stops.name: Turkestan and, by report, India — the farthest road
stops.campa: Beyond Khwarizm the road runs out onto the steppe of Turkestan, into the Turkic marches where the settled Persian world gives way to tents and horse-herds, and tradition carries Attar further still, into India, though later scholars will find no firm ground for the claim and some doubt it outright. Attar himself leaves no ledger of these farthest miles, only the accumulated habit, wherever he has gone, of listening more than teaching. He turns back at last toward Khorasan a middle-aged man loaded with a decade of gathered sayings and no book yet begun, the whole world's report of holiness carried home to a closed shop in Shadiyakh.

stops.name: Shadiyakh, return to the shop, the notebooks of the road
stops.campa: Attar returns to Shadiyakh and to the shop that has stood shut or minded by kin through all his years of travel, and reopens it, dispensing remedies by day as he did as a young man, a druggist again in trade though a different man in everything else. But now beside the scales on the counter lie notebooks: sayings of Bayazid, of Hallaj, of Rabia, of a hundred lesser saints, gathered on every road from Bastam to the Turkic steppe. In the hours the shop allows him, he begins to set them into order, the first sentences of a memorial no one has asked him to write.

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the Tazkirat al-Awliya
stops.campa: Over years at the counter, Attar completes the Tazkirat al-Awliya, the Memorial of God's Friends, seventy-two lives of the Sufi saints from Ja'far al-Sadiq to Hallaj, rendered in plain Persian prose so that readers without Arabic can reach what he calls a commentary on the Qur'an itself in everything but name. He gives fifteen reasons for the labor in his own preface, chief among them that the Koran and the Traditions, locked in Arabic, are closed to most of his countrymen, while the sayings of the saints, translated, open the same door in the believer's own tongue.
stops.quote: The Koran and the Traditions cannot be understood without knowledge of Arabic, wherefore most people are unable to profit by them; and the Sayings of the Saints, which form a commentary on the Koran and the Traditions, were likewise uttered, for the most part, in Arabic. Consequently the author has translated them into Persian, in order that they may become accessible to all.
stops.quote_source: R. A. Nicholson, rendering Attar's own reason from the preface to the Tazkirat al-Awliya (introduction to Muslim Saints and Mystics)

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the Divan
stops.campa: Alongside the prose memorial, Attar sets down his Divan, several thousand lines of lyric ghazal and qasida in the old Persian forms, love-poems whose Beloved slides, verse by verse, between an earthly face and God, in the manner every Sufi poet after him will imitate. Unlike the didactic mathnavis that will make his lasting name, the Divan shows the craftsman's hand alone, sound and image worked for their own sake, and later poets, Rumi among them, will read it less for doctrine than for the sheer working of Persian syllables into music before they turn to his other books for guidance.

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the Asrar-nama
stops.campa: Attar composes the Asrar-nama, the Book of Secrets, a shorter mathnavi of anecdotes and homilies strung on the string of Sufi doctrine, meant, he says himself, as an introduction for the beginner before the harder roads of his later books. It will outlive its modest billing: a quarter-century on, a fleeing scholar from Balkh will pass through Nishapur with a small son, and Attar will press this very book, the beginner's book, into the child's hands as a parting gift, not knowing, or perhaps knowing exactly, that the boy will one day set fire to the hearts of the world's lovers.

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the Elahi-nama
stops.campa: In the Elahi-nama, the Book of the Divine, Attar frames his teaching as a caliph questioning his six sons on the heart's true desire: one wants the fairy king's daughter, one magic, one the world-revealing cup of Jamshid, one the water of life, one Solomon's ring over the demons, one the philosopher's stone. To each in turn the father shows the desire is a veil over a better one: the fairy princess is the son's own purified soul, the cup of Jamshid the moment truth is mistaken for its mirror, the ring of Solomon nothing more than contentment with what a man already has.

stops.name: Shadiyakh, the Mosibat-nama
stops.campa: In the Mosibat-nama, the Book of Afflictions, Attar sends a solitary wayfarer, the salek-e fekrat, the traveller of Thought, through forty stations of creation in search of relief: he questions Gabriel and the angels, the throne and its pedestal, the tablet and the pen, paradise and hell, sun and moon, the four elements, the mountains and seas, the plants, the animals, the jinn, mankind, the prophets, and at last the faculties of the mind. Each confesses it does not hold what he seeks. Only the universal soul answers him: cast yourself into the ocean of the soul and be utterly effaced, for what you want is nowhere but in you.

stops.name: Shadiyakh, Mantiq al-Tayr — the hoopoe calls the birds
stops.campa: In what will become his masterwork, the Mantiq al-Tayr, the Language of the Birds, Attar gathers every bird of the earth in council: they have no king, and the wisest among them, the hoopoe, who once carried letters between Solomon and Sheba, tells them of a king they do have, though none has seen him: the Simurgh, whose feather once fell over China and set every heart there to painting it. Thousands answer the call to seek him; the hoopoe warns that seven valleys of fire and thorn lie between the birds and any sight of their king, and most will not survive the crossing.
stops.quote: The world's birds gathered for their conference / And said: 'Our constitution makes no sense. / All nations in the world require a king; / How is it we alone have no such thing?'
stops.quote_source: Mantiq al-Tayr (The Conference of the Birds), the birds assemble, trans. Afkham Darbandi & Dick Davis
